> They allow authors to provide context or cite sources without disrupting the main narrative flow.

Obviously, I disagree with this statement 😄

From a reading experience perspective, footnotes do have many problems and should not be used in many situations. However, many of the issues mentioned in Jake's article, such as accessibility and user experience, will be easier to mitigate with dedicated footnote markup.

Some websites, such as academic journals, require footnotes when displayed on the web.
Wouldn't reusing `rel` be enough? `rel=footnote` was even considered back in HTML 4.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/relations.html

> Wouldn't reusing `rel` be enough? `rel=footnote` was even considered back in HTML 4.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/relations.html

Yeah, it is logical and has historical precedent.

However, IIUC it would be insufficient because it only solves one part of a multi-faceted problem. It addresses the *relationship of the link* but fails to address the more fundamental issues of *text association* and *authoring automation*.

The primary advantage of `rel` is that it adds a clear semantic meaning to the link itself. A user agent, search engine, or assistive technology could parse `rel="footnote"` and understand that this is not a generic hyperlink but one that points to an annotation. This is a clear improvement over the current situation.

Despite the benefit above, it fails to resolve the most critical problems that motivated the creation of this proposal: it does not fix the broken association with the content.

This proposal solves this by providing a semantic container for the footnote content, allowing user agents to identify it as such (e.g., for styling, accessibility, or other kinds of processing).

Also, another goal of a this proposal is to simplify the authoring process. The `rel="footnote"` approach provides no automation benefits. The author must still manually number the footnotes  (`[1]`, `[2]`, `[3]`), manually manage `id`s and ensure they match the `href`, manually create reciprocal links to return the user to the point of reference, and manually re-number all subsequent footnotes if one is inserted or removed in the middle of the document.

This proposal allows the user agent to handle all of this automatically via CSS counters and built-in behaviors, reducing authoring effort and the potential for error.

@xfq have you looked into the expanded [`aria-details`](https://pr-preview.s3.amazonaws.com/w3c/aria/pull/1136.html#aria-details) definition in ARIA 1.3? It references a [`doc-footnote` role defined in DPUB-ARIA-1.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/dpub-aria-1.0/#doc-footnote). The general exploration there was spearheaded by @aleventhal in the https://github.com/aleventhal/aria-annotations repo which links to some UX related ephemera that might be worth exploring. The general aim was improving accessibility of annotations not just in reading environments, but also in editing environments (such as Google Docs).

Thanks @xfq for raising this with the Publishing Maintenance WG, which maintains EPUB and Publication Manifest, two standards for digital publishing using web technologies. Footnotes/endnotes have been a long-standing use case and challenge in the publishing industry, and the current state described by @xfq is driven largely by publishing's work on things like DPUB-ARIA. Even with all this work, footnotes/endnotes remain a huge challenge in EPUB and digital publishing, with different platforms and different publishers implementing things in different ways, resulting in very different user experiences. Having an easier, more consistent way to identify note content would be a massive benefit for publishing stakeholders across the board. While it's true that some of the examples that @jakearchibald mention _might_ work for publishing, such as the use of `
` or `
`, I think one huge thing is being missed about the user experience of superscript numerals in text and the benefit for one of the cases mentioned in the blog post: skipability. Because footnotes/endnotes are an established pattern, we don't need to overengineer them, people are familiar, you don't need to over-explain them, and they serve a very important purpose in books and articles. There are also practical reasons we can't use a solution like `
` for footnote content. In paginated content, particularly on eInk devices (which are dominant in EPUB rendering), opening details would result in a re-render, disrupting pagination and potentially overlapping the page area, making the content challenging to read. The most common affordance reading systems have developed to handle footnote/endnote content is the dialog popup, where instead of navigating to the note location, a dialog appears containing the footnote content (see screenshots below). This is where the current challenge most often appears, because reading systems currently have to juggle multiple ways of identifying footnote/endnote content due to the confusion over the best method. All this is to say that we shouldn't be too flippant about considering a proposal like this, even though it is derived from the dark ages of print. There is a reason why print publishers did not take some of the approaches recommended in @jakearchibald's post, some of them practical, some of them stylistic. Sure, in some cases, inline notation (like this) might be fine, in others an aside might be just as effective, but superscript notations remain popular for a reason, especially in cases where citation is important but readability should be preserved.

Thanks @xfq for raising this. I am commenting with my former academic publisher hat (and former EPUB chair hat). I also have a lot of personal familiarity with interlingual texts. +1 to @reidmore-online's comments.

Academia: Another perspective is the world of academia. The footnotes and endnotes are often viewed as a separate body of work. Even if this has to do with the way things were formatted 200 years ago, we will not change academic publishing by telling them to get with the times. It's rooted in requirements from organizations like NIH and the number of citations required to get tenure at universities. Even if it's a separate body, there still needs to be the connection to the main text, as explained by others.

Translations and Glosses: When a work is translated or explained, there are often footnotes that explain the translator's methodology or specific terminology choices. Think back to your Folger edition of Shakespeare with annotations on the recto page. You don't want the explanations interrupting the flow of text, and you absolutely want them anchored to the correct word. The [Tufts Perseus library](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/) has some examples. See https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0046:chapter=16 or [The Odyssey](http://data.perseus.org/texts/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc1). A more complicated work, like the Bible or the Talmud, has thousands of commentators in multiple languages. Each commentary is a gloss on a specific word or group of words. I am familiar with online tools, such as https://www.sefaria.org/texts, that do a good job of interlinear translation and minor annotation. I have only seen native apps that layer original text, glosses, translations, and commentary. (These may not interest the average web developer, but religious books is one of the few markets that is always successful.)

Like @TzviyaSiegman says, there are uses for footnotes in publishing that shouldn’t be ignored based on personal preferences. 

It is worth exploring adding these two new elements. 

Currently, an author must wrap the content of a pop-up note in an` <aside>` tag. It works reasonably well in straightforward documents.

However, in a more complex document it can conflict with a pull quote or call-out box. [Like in the example Mozilla uses here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/aside) 

A dedicated element for notes and note references would let `<aside>` be used for other content.

Automatic numbering of footnote references would be a great timesaver and one less worry when doing QA.

I also wonder what uses we could find for associating the footnotes with a span of text beyond the number code. Perhaps exported footnotes could include the span text improving clarity and continuity.

To be clear, my views on footnotes are absolutely personal opinion, and mostly aimed at frustrating experiences I had reading blogs that relied on them for making some content 'optional'. In my blog post, I wasn't representing anyone's views except my own.

One concern with the proposal is that it uses the general name "note" for the element but seems to bind the expectation for its use to footnotes. That could get confusing as it doesn't take into account that ARIA proper already has a note role.

The reason DPUB-ARIA has doc-footnote is to differentiate the cases, as there are many kinds of notes that aren't footnotes.

One other consideration: if the note element is equivalent of a list item, it might be problematic to have an implicit mapping to doc-footnote.

doc-endnote was added to DPUB-ARIA to serve as a list item role, but modules can't satisfy ARIA core role requirements so it ended up being deprecated. A section marked as doc-endnotes also can't contain elements of the role doc-footnote, so that could pose another problem.

But if a new element gets added, I suspect it wouldn't be right to have it mapping to a semantic from a module like DPUB-ARIA. It'd probably be a case of having to create a new unprefixed role in ARIA proper. Whatever that becomes is just complicated by the existing roles and expectations on them.

>This proposal introduces a new set of elements, `<noteref>` and `<note>`, to give footnotes first-class citizenship on the web.

Dedicated elements could be a tool for standardizing footnotes across reading systems. I’m currently [testing ereaders’ various footnote specs cross-platform](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Gv9uXS-tw9hEcwPzCuP4p8W3cPN1MomatSLmB_UimQc/edit?usp=sharing) (ie. Does Apple’s method work on a Kindle?). I haven’t yet found a single method that is universally reliable for pop-up notes.

>One other consideration: if the note element is equivalent of a list item, it might be problematic to have an implicit mapping to doc-footnote.

So far, pop-up style notes work best when they are each in their own (non-linear) document. If `<note>` is a subset of `<ol>` this would break. Or we would have to nest each note inside its own list inside its own document, which seems unnecessarily complex.

It is worth thinking through footnote usage in pop-ups, as that is considered a better user experience than bi-directional linked notes, which move a reader to a new place in an ebook.

> and provide users with dedicated navigation commands to jump between references and their corresponding notes, and back again

Forgetting EPUB reading systems' general lack of back buttons for a minute, this has also proven problematic because there can be a many-to-one relationship between references and a note. People often read the notes after finishing a chapter and then want to find their way easily back to the reference, but that becomes difficult if there's more than one reference. That's why we introduced baclink/doc-backlink to provide hyperlinks to the references, but it's always been kind of kludgey. It would be interesting if there were a better way to provide this functionality that wouldn't rely on an assistive technology, but I also don't expect that reading systems/browsers will want to implement an interface to cycle through possible destinations. It's not a problem that is particular to accessibility.

> One concern with the proposal is that it uses the general name "note" for the element but seems to bind the expectation for its use to footnotes. That could get confusing as it doesn't take into account that ARIA proper already has a note role.

> The reason DPUB-ARIA has doc-footnote is to differentiate the cases, as there are many kinds of notes that aren't footnotes.

Indeed, we could consider renaming `<note>` to `<footnote>`.

I think @mattgarrish's concern below can be addressed a different way than more narrowly scoping the element to a narrower use case:
> One concern with the proposal is that it uses the general name "note" for the element but seems to bind the expectation for its use to footnotes.

Addressing it by narrowing the scope (i.e. "we could consider renaming `<note>` to `<footnote>`.") would seem to flip the concern the wrong way around.

Instead, perhaps the new `<note>` element should not be explicitly forced into being a "footnote" but instead augmented (when desired) with footnote-like affordances via additional attributes/roles/etc.

Sorry I feel like this might be sidetracking based on a potential misunderstanding, but...

I know that we are in the midst of trying to align link kinds and behaviors and IDL as much as possible between HTML, SVG and MathML - and then working with the Sanitizer and so on to make sense of it safely, etc... This seems like it is effectively trying to create another kind of link with just some light semantic/styling differences. I'd like to understand better why `rel` or something doesn't work? In your reply you say this proposal lets the browser automatically do automation ...

> Also, another goal of a this proposal is to simplify the authoring process. The rel="footnote" approach provides no automation benefits. The author must still manually number the footnotes ([1], [2], [3]), manually manage ids and ensure they match the href, manually create reciprocal links to return the user to the point of reference, and manually re-number all subsequent footnotes if one is inserted or removed in the middle of the document.

But the example you posted does manually number the footnotes and manage the ids, so I'm trying to understand that better.... I don't see why we can't apply styles to links with rel?

> fwiw, i'd submit that a [`note`](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.3/#note), and dpub ARIA footnote/endnote roles are different enough that it's probably better they be kept as separate elements, rather than have a single element that would change its semantics/role mappings depending on the attributes applied to it. > > > Lastly, the "backlink" need could possibly be addressed by using the [for attribute](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/for) > > any thoughts on what the keyboard behavior would be for something like this? I can't speak to @BigBlueHat's proposal exactly for this, but speaking in terms of reading experiences and the "current" experience, I think the keyboard behaviour would be similar to the behaviour for popovers/dialogs, where focus lands on the "trigger" (superscript number), if activated a popover/dialog opens and focus is pulled to that, with a close button/ESC bringing the focus back to the trigger? That's the ideal scenario. In cases where we are doing a more typical link action, i.e. the trigger goes to another location on the page/book and back again, I've seen examples in EPUB where the superscript is a link, so receives focus, on activation they are brought to the new location (usually another file/page), and in that location there is a link back to the original location, usually as the leading numeral in a list of footnotes, or even more obviously as link text that says "back to [page]". The same book I used in my screenshots above does this too, but it's not a consistent pattern.
